item.title: R' Efryim Dovid Gruskin
item.description:
Who he is in this story

R’ Efryim Dovid Gruskin, Mrs. Manya Ort’s brother-in-law, described by the site as a former Rosh Yeshiva. The original site addresses him in two open letters — asking him to reflect on the counsel he has given his sister-in-law, and challenging his reported description of her as “penniless” and “starving.”

The first letter: a call to reflect

The letter grants that his advice was surely given with her best interests in mind, then asks him to look at where the road traveled under that advice has led — “Can you honestly say that it has led in the direction of peace, closure and resolution of the conflicts that have been tearing this family apart?”

item.title: The Adler Story
item.description:
What happened, according to the documents

R’ Avraham Ort’s mother passed away in November 1999. In January 2000, Mrs. Manya Ort moved $350,000 out of her late mother-in-law’s account at Discount Bank and wired it to an Israel account of Mrs. Ort Sr. that already held $250,000. She then gave the combined $600,000 to her cousin R’ Ira (Yitzchak) Adler of Monsey, NY, with instructions to disburse it to “a yeshiva” — which yeshiva was never named.

item.title: The Brodericks
item.description:
Who they are in this story

Mrs. Soro Rochel (Sarah) Broderick, a married daughter of R’ Avrohom Ort, and her husband R’ Ranaan Broderick. The original site’s correspondence — signed “the true friends of the Brodericks” — lays out three financial issues and a parallel dispute over whether the family would submit to a Din Torah.

The three financial issues, as the site presents them

  1. Custodial accounts. Over $180,000 in cash that Mrs. Broderick acquired by taking ownership of custodial accounts her father had established in her name. A Salomon Smith Barney letter of September 2002, confirming the account history going back to December 1999, is cataloged: catalog entry — view the letter .

  2. Real estate that R’ Avrohom inherited from his parents and placed in her name as a legal tax shelter, which she assumed control of.

  3. Substantial income generated by the above.

item.title: The Steinbergs
item.description:
Who they are in this story

Rabbi Yisroel Steinberg and Mrs. Miriam Steinberg of Lakewood. The original site describes Mrs. Steinberg as Mrs. Manya Ort’s friend since kindergarten, and addresses the couple in a series of open letters — arguing that they publicly portrayed Mrs. Ort as “penniless” and “starving,” and urging them to call on her to bring the dispute to a Beis Din.

The $3,000 chesed loan

According to the site, Rabbi Steinberg — then president of the g’mach of Cong. Zichron Shneur — arranged a $3,000 “chesed loan” for Mrs. Ort. The site quotes his July 2002 deposition: “she said she needed $3,000 and… I wrote out the check.”

item.title: Who Went to Court, and Who to Beis Din?
item.description:
The question

As the original site frames it: the impression from Mrs. Ort’s camp is that only after R’ Avrohom took her to secular court and lost is he now insisting on Beis Din — and since he accepted binding arbitration, why is he complaining? The page answers with documents.

Who filed first

Page 8 of the Final Arbitration Ruling, headed “Procedural History,” states that Mrs. Ort filed the divorce complaint on February 4, 2000, accompanied by an Order to Show Cause freezing assets — including the children’s and the Dove Foundation’s assets — and that a March 6, 2000 order continued the restraint: catalog entry — view .
